read.sections.0.heading.source: Trade links places into a network
read.sections.0.heading.back: Trade joins places into a network

read.sections.0.text.note: 'network' as 'mạng lưới', 'port' as 'cảng', 'link' as 'mắt xích'. 'Trade' is first defined as 'đưa hàng hóa đi để nhận lại hàng hóa khác hoặc tiền'. Check that 'buôn bán' and 'đổi' (swap) are used naturally. | Review: 'mắt xích' (link in a chain) is used for 'links' of the network; check it is clear to 10-year-olds. Also 'Con đường Tơ lụa' is singular though English has 'Silk Roads' (the text explains it is many routes).
read.sections.0.text.source: Trade means giving goods to get other goods or money back. Goods are things people make or grow, like tea, jars or cloth. In the fictional network, the hill village sends tea by cart to Riverstone. Boats carry the tea and Riverstone's clay jars down the river to Coastport. At this port, traders swap them for cloth and salt from visiting ships. No single trader makes the whole journey. Each person carries the goods along one part of the route. Together, these links form a network. If the river is too low for boats, traders must find another way.
read.sections.0.text.back: Trade means sending goods in order to receive other goods or money. Goods are things people make or grow, such as tea, clay jars or cloth. In this fictional network, the hill village sends tea by cart to Riverstone. Boats carry the tea and Riverstone's clay jars down the river to Coastport. At this port, merchants swap them for cloth and salt from the ships that stop by. No single merchant goes the whole journey. Each person carries goods along one stretch of the route. These links together make a network. If the river water is too low for boats, the merchants must find another way.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Trade means giving something to get something back. Goods are things people make or grow. A cart takes tea from the hill village to Riverstone. Boats take tea and jars to Coastport. At the port, people swap them for cloth and salt. No one person makes the whole trip. Each person does one part of the route. All the links make a network. If the river is low, traders need a new way.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Trade means giving one thing to get one thing back. Goods are things people make or grow. A cart carries tea from the hill village to Riverstone. Boats carry tea and clay jars to Coastport. At the port, people swap them for cloth and salt. Nobody goes the whole stretch of the way. Each person does one stretch of the route. All the links make a network. If the river is dry, merchants need to find a new way.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Real trade routes crossed land, sea and desert
read.sections.1.heading.back: Real trade routes crossed land, sea and desert

read.sections.1.text.note: 'Con đường Tơ lụa' is singular in Vietnamese, but the text says it is many routes, not one road. 'bán đảo Ả Rập' for Arabia. 'Đế quốc Mali' for the Mali Empire. 'Gió mùa' for monsoon winds. 'Trung Á', 'Trung Đông', 'Đông Nam Á', 'Ấn Độ Dương' are the usual forms. Place names are not contested here, but a native speaker should check them.
read.sections.1.text.source: Real trade networks were much bigger. The Silk Roads began more than 2,000 years ago. They were many land and sea routes, not one road, and they linked China with Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. Silk from China travelled west, while horses and glass travelled east. On the Indian Ocean, sailors used the monsoon winds, which change direction twice a year. Ships could sail out on one wind and come home on the next. Ports in East Africa, Arabia, India, Southeast Asia and China traded spices, cloth, gold and fine pottery. In Africa, camels crossed the Sahara Desert, carrying salt south and gold north. Timbuktu, in the Mali Empire, grew rich from this trade.
read.sections.1.text.back: Real trade networks were much bigger. The Silk Road began more than 2,000 years ago. It was many routes over land and sea, not a single road, joining China with Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. Silk from China went west, while horses and glass went east. On the Indian Ocean, sailors made use of the monsoon, a wind that changes direction twice a year. Ships could set out with one season's wind and return with the next season's wind. Ports in East Africa, the Arabian peninsula, India, Southeast Asia and China traded spices, cloth, gold and fine pottery. In Africa, camel caravans crossed the Sahara desert, bringing salt south and gold north. Timbuktu, in the Mali Empire, became rich thanks to this trade.

read.sections.1.simpler.note: 'Chúng nối Trung Quốc với những vùng đất xa về phía tây' simplifies 'Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe'. Check it is not too vague.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Real trade networks were much bigger. The Silk Roads began over 2,000 years ago. They were many land and sea routes. They linked China to lands far to the west. Silk went west, and horses went east. On the Indian Ocean, ships used winds that change twice a year. So ships could sail out and come back. In Africa, camels crossed the Sahara Desert. They took salt south and gold north. This trade made Timbuktu rich.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Real trade networks were much bigger. The Silk Road began from more than 2,000 years ago. It was many routes on land and sea. They joined China with far-away lands to the west. Silk went west, while horses went east. On the Indian Ocean, ships used winds that change direction twice a year. Thanks to this, ships could set out and then come back. In Africa, camels crossed the Sahara desert. They brought salt south and gold north. This trade made Timbuktu rich.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Trade moved ideas as well as goods
read.sections.2.heading.back: Trade moved ideas, not only goods

read.sections.2.text.note: Sensitive: one sentence on enslaved people ('những người bị bắt làm nô lệ, tức là những người bị ép làm việc cho người khác'). Check it is factual, short and gentle. Religion is only mentioned as something that travelled ('tôn giáo'); keep it neutral.
read.sections.2.text.source: Traders carried ideas as well as goods. Paper was first made in China, and papermaking later spread along the routes to Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. Religions and languages also travelled with traders. Timbuktu became famous for its books and teachers. In Riverstone, the potter's note shows an idea on the move, because a visiting trader shared a new way to decorate jars. But trade did not help everyone equally. Some traders grew rich, while others lost out. On some routes, traders also bought and sold enslaved people, who were forced to work for others.
read.sections.2.text.back: Merchants carried ideas as well as goods. Paper was first made in China, and papermaking then spread along the routes to Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. Religions and languages also travelled with merchants. Timbuktu became famous thanks to books and teachers. In Riverstone, the potter's note shows an idea moving, because a passing merchant shared a way to decorate jars anew. But trade did not help everyone equally. Some merchants became rich, while others were at a loss. On some routes, merchants also bought and sold people who had been taken as slaves, that is, people forced to work for others.

read.sections.2.simpler.note: Sensitive: 'Những người này bị bắt làm nô lệ và không được tự do.' Check tone and clarity.
read.sections.2.simpler.source: People in China made the first paper. Traders took this idea to other lands. Religions and languages moved along the routes too. In Riverstone, a trader shows the potter a new way to make jars pretty. That is an idea on the move. But trade did not help everyone. Some traders got rich. Others lost out. On some routes, traders bought and sold people. These people were enslaved and not free.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: The Chinese people first made paper. Merchants brought this idea to other lands. Religions and languages also went along the routes. In Riverstone, a merchant showed the potter how to make a more beautiful jar. That is an idea moving. But trade did not help everybody. Some merchants got rich. Others were at a loss. On some routes, merchants bought and sold people. These people were taken as slaves and were not free.

write.example.source: First, the jar is made by a potter in Riverstone. Next, a boat trader carries it down the river to Coastport, with tea from the hill village. The places are linked by a cart road, a river and the sea. At the port, a trader swaps the jar and the tea for cloth and salt. An idea could travel when a sailor sees the pattern on the jar and copies it at home. This shows that trade can move ideas as well as goods.
write.example.back: First, the jar was made by a potter in Riverstone. Next, a merchant travelling by boat carried it down the river to Coastport, along with tea from the hill village. The places are joined by a cart road, a river and the sea. At the port, a merchant swapped the jar and the tea for cloth and salt. An idea can move when a sailor sees the pattern on the jar and copies it in the place where that person lives. This shows that trade can move ideas, not only goods.

watch.summary.source: This animated video tells the story of the Silk Road. It explains how, more than 2,000 years ago, trade began to grow between China and lands to the west. The Silk Road was not one road. It was a network of many routes that linked towns across Asia to the Middle East and Europe. Most traders did not travel the whole way. They carried goods along one part, then passed them on to other traders. Silk, spices, horses and many other goods moved along the routes. Ideas moved too. Beliefs, languages, art and new ways of making things spread from place to place. Some of these changes still shape how people live today. The video calls the Silk Road an early 'world wide web', because it linked so many people.
watch.summary.back: This animated video tells the story of the Silk Road. The video explains that more than 2,000 years ago, trade between China and the lands to the west began to grow strong. The Silk Road was not a single road. It was a network of many routes joining towns across Asia with the Middle East and Europe. Most merchants did not go the whole distance. They carried goods one stretch, then passed them on to other merchants. Silk, spices, horses and many other goods moved along the routes. Ideas moved too. Beliefs, languages, art and new ways of making things spread from place to place. Some of those changes still affect how people live today. The video calls the Silk Road an ancient global network, because it joined very many people together.
